tips.title: Four-fifths and one-fifth
tips.body: **About 80% nitrogen** and **about 20% oxygen**, with **small proportions of other gases** including carbon dioxide, water vapour and the noble gases. Said as fractions: **four-fifths** and **one-fifth**. These proportions have held for about **200 million years**.

tips.title: Say "one theory suggests"
tips.body: The spec is careful that these are **theories**, because the **evidence is limited** by the **4.6 billion year** timescale. Questions ask you to **evaluate** competing accounts, so write *one theory suggests* rather than stating the early atmosphere as fact.

tips.title: Oxygen up and carbon dioxide down, one cause
tips.body: **Photosynthesis** did both at once: it **took in carbon dioxide** and **gave out oxygen**. So the two great changes in the atmosphere are two halves of a single equation, which is far easier to hold than two separate stories.

tips.title: Carbon dioxide had three exits
tips.body: **Dissolving in the oceans** (then precipitating as **carbonates**), **photosynthesis**, and being **locked into sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels**. A question asking how carbon dioxide decreased wants more than one of these.

tips.title: Mars and Venus are the comparison
tips.body: The early atmosphere **may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today**: **mainly carbon dioxide** with **little or no oxygen**. Naming those two planets is the spec's own comparison and is worth a mark.

why.matters:
The air is not a given. It is the **output** of four and a half billion years of chemistry, and most of the interesting part was done by living things: the oxygen you are breathing is a waste product, and the carbon dioxide that is missing was buried.

It is also where this course teaches you to handle thin evidence. Nobody was there, almost nothing survives from the first billion years, and the honest answer is a **theory** to be weighed rather than a fact to be recited.

examples.title: Mars still has the atmosphere we started with
examples.body:
One theory is that the early Earth had an atmosphere mainly of carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen — and you can go and look at one. Mars and Venus are both **mostly carbon dioxide** today, and neither has life to change it.

That comparison is the evidence, and it also shows what the oxygen here needs explaining. Four-fifths nitrogen and one-fifth oxygen is not what a planet gets by default. It is what a planet gets after two billion years of photosynthesis.

visual.alt: A table comparing the atmospheres of Earth, Mars and Venus: Earth with only a trace of carbon dioxide and about a fifth oxygen, against Mars and Venus which are both about ninety-five per cent carbon dioxide with almost no oxygen

examples.title: The oxygen you are breathing is waste
examples.body:
Algae in the oceans were not making oxygen for anybody. They were making sugar, and oxygen is what was left over — an inconvenience so reactive that it poisoned most of the life that existed at the time.

The same equation explains the other great change. Every molecule of oxygen released came from a molecule of carbon dioxide taken in, so the rise of one and the fall of the other are not two stories. They are the two sides of one arrow.

visual.alt: The photosynthesis equation, six carbon dioxide and six water becoming glucose and six oxygen, the single reaction that both removed carbon dioxide from the early atmosphere and put the oxygen into it

examples.title: Where the carbon dioxide went
examples.body:
An atmosphere that was mostly carbon dioxide is now a trace of it, and the carbon did not leave the planet. It is under your feet.

It dissolved in the oceans and came out as **carbonate** — chalk and limestone are a former atmosphere, shell by shell. It was built into plants and animals that were buried and became **coal, oil and gas**. Which is the awkward part of the story: burning a fossil fuel is putting a piece of the ancient atmosphere back where it came from.

boxes.title: Into rock
boxes.body: Chalk and limestone are made of that carbonate.

boxes.title: Into fossil fuels
boxes.body: Buried before it could rot. We dig it up.

visual.alt: Four boxes round a centre reading where the carbon dioxide went: dissolved into the oceans, precipitated as the carbonate that chalk and limestone are made of, built into living things by photosynthesis, and buried as fossil fuels

steps.title: The atmosphere today
steps.body:
**For 200 million years, the proportions of different gases in the atmosphere have been much the same as they are today:**

- about **four-fifths**, approximately **80%**, **nitrogen**
- about **one-fifth**, approximately **20%**, **oxygen**
- **small proportions of various other gases**, including **carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases**

**Two hundred million years is a long time but not most of Earth's history.** The Earth is about **4.6 billion years** old, so the atmosphere we breathe has been stable for only the most recent few per cent of it. Everything before that was very different — which is what the rest of this topic is about.

**Be careful with the word *small*.** Carbon dioxide is a **small proportion** of the atmosphere, well under 1%. That it matters enormously despite being scarce is a point the greenhouse topic returns to; here the point is simply that nitrogen and oxygen between them account for essentially all of the air.

**The fractions are worth knowing as fractions**, because questions sometimes give data as proportions rather than percentages. Four-fifths is 80%, and one-fifth is 20%.

steps.title: The early atmosphere
steps.body:
**Theories about what was in the Earth's early atmosphere and how the atmosphere was formed have changed and developed over time.** The spec is deliberate about this, and so should your answers be.

**Why the evidence is limited:** the timescale is **4.6 billion years**. Nothing was recorded, almost nothing has survived unaltered, and so scientists work from indirect evidence. That is why **competing theories** exist and why questions ask you to **evaluate** rather than recall.

**One theory suggests** the following:

- During the **first billion years** of the Earth's existence there was **intense volcanic activity**.
- This **released gases that formed the early atmosphere**, and **water vapour that condensed to form the oceans**.
- At the start, the atmosphere **may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today**: **mainly carbon dioxide**, with **little or no oxygen**.
- **Volcanoes also produced nitrogen**, which **gradually built up** in the atmosphere.
- There **may have been small proportions of methane and ammonia**.

**Then the oceans changed things.** **When the oceans formed, carbon dioxide dissolved in the water and carbonates were precipitated, producing sediments** — and this **reduced the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere**.

**Nitrogen is the gas that simply accumulated.** It is very **unreactive**, so once volcanoes had released it there was little to remove it. Carbon dioxide had several exits; nitrogen had almost none. That is why nitrogen is now the most abundant gas in the air — not because most was released, but because least was taken away.

**No knowledge of other theories is required**, but the phrase *one theory suggests* should still appear in your answer.

steps.title: How oxygen increased and carbon dioxide decreased
steps.body:
**Both great changes have the same cause, and it is one equation.**

$$\mathrm{6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2}$$

**Algae and plants produced the oxygen that is now in the atmosphere by photosynthesis**, and the same process **decreased the percentage of carbon dioxide**. One reaction, two effects.

**The timeline the spec gives:**

- **Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago**, and **soon after this oxygen appeared in the atmosphere**.
- **Over the next billion years plants evolved**, and the **percentage of oxygen gradually increased** to a level that **enabled animals to evolve**.

**That last clause is the point of the whole story.** Animals could not exist until there was enough oxygen, and the oxygen was put there by algae and plants. The atmosphere is not a backdrop to life; it was made by it.

**Carbon dioxide decreased three ways**, and a question asking how wants more than one:

1. **Dissolving in the oceans**, where **carbonates were precipitated** as **sediments**.
2. **Photosynthesis** by algae and plants.
3. The **formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels that contain carbon**.

**How those deposits formed** is examinable:

- **Limestone** — from the **shells and skeletons** of sea creatures, which were made of carbonate, settling and being compressed into **sedimentary rock**.
- **Coal** — from **plant material**, buried in conditions where it could not fully decay, then compressed over millions of years.
- **Crude oil and natural gas** — from **plankton**, tiny marine organisms, buried in **mud** on the sea floor and subjected to **high pressure and temperature** over millions of years, in the **absence of oxygen**.

**So the carbon in the air did not vanish; it was locked away** — in rock and in fossil fuels. Which is precisely why burning fossil fuels puts it back.

steps.title: Evaluating the evidence
steps.body:
**The spec asks you to interpret evidence and evaluate different theories about the Earth's early atmosphere, given appropriate information.** So this is a skills question, not a recall one, and it has a predictable shape.

**Why the evidence is limited:**

- The timescale is about **4.6 billion years**, so there are **no direct measurements** and no records.
- Rocks and other evidence have been **altered** over that time.
- Evidence is **indirect** — trapped gases, the composition of ancient rocks, comparisons with other planets.

**What makes one theory better supported than another:** how much **evidence** it accounts for, whether that evidence comes from **more than one independent source**, and whether it has been **peer reviewed**.

**How to write an evaluation.** Give **both sides and then decide**:

1. What the evidence **supports**.
2. What it **cannot settle**, and why.
3. A **judgement**, with the reason it depends on.

An answer that lists points without reaching a conclusion has not evaluated anything — and that is the commonest way marks are lost on this style of question.

**A worked example of the reasoning.** Mars and Venus today have atmospheres of **mainly carbon dioxide** with little oxygen. That is **consistent** with the theory that Earth's early atmosphere was similar, since all three formed in similar ways at similar times. But it is **not proof**: the planets differ in size, temperature and distance from the Sun, and Earth alone developed oceans and life. So the comparison **supports** the theory without **confirming** it — which is exactly the sort of sentence these questions are asking for.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**One equation explains both great changes.** Photosynthesis **took in carbon dioxide** and **gave out oxygen**, so the fall of one and the rise of the other are not two stories but two halves of the same one. An answer that gives photosynthesis for the oxygen and forgets it for the carbon dioxide has told half of it.

**Nitrogen won by not being removed.** It is very **unreactive**, so once volcanoes had released it there was almost nothing to take it out again. Carbon dioxide, by contrast, had **three exits** — dissolving in the oceans, photosynthesis, and burial in **rocks and fossil fuels**. Nitrogen is the most abundant gas because it **accumulated**, not because most was released, and saying that is a better answer than *volcanoes made a lot of it*.

**The carbon was locked away, not destroyed.** **Limestone** holds the carbonate from **shells and skeletons**; **coal** holds **plant material**; **crude oil and natural gas** hold **plankton**. Making that explicit sets up the greenhouse topic exactly: burning fossil fuels **returns** carbon that took millions of years to remove, which is why the rate matters as much as the amount.

**Say *one theory suggests*.** The spec stresses that theories **have changed and developed over time** and that the evidence is **limited by the 4.6 billion year timescale**. An answer that states the early atmosphere as established fact has missed what the question is testing.

**Evaluate means decide.** Give what the evidence **supports**, what it **cannot settle**, and then a **judgement** with its reason. The Mars and Venus comparison is the model: it is **consistent** with the theory, but those planets differ from Earth in size, temperature and distance from the Sun, so it **supports without confirming**.

**And the oxygen story has a consequence worth stating.** The percentage rose **gradually** over about a billion years to a level that **enabled animals to evolve**. Life did not simply appear in a suitable atmosphere; it **made** one. That is the sentence that turns a list of dates into an explanation.

questions.prompt: Describe how the Earth's atmosphere changed from its early composition to what it is today, and explain the causes of the main changes.
questions.solution:
**One theory suggests** that during the **first billion years** of the Earth's existence there was **intense volcanic activity**, which **released the gases that formed the early atmosphere**. That atmosphere was **mainly carbon dioxide** with **little or no oxygen**, and **may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today**. Volcanoes also released **nitrogen**, and there **may have been small proportions of methane and ammonia**. It is worth saying *one theory suggests*, because the **evidence is limited** by the **4.6 billion year** timescale.

The volcanoes also released a great deal of **water vapour**. As the Earth cooled, this **condensed to form the oceans**. That had an immediate effect on the atmosphere: **carbon dioxide dissolved in the water**, and **carbonates were precipitated, producing sediments**, so the amount of carbon dioxide in the air began to fall.

The larger change came from life. **Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago** by **photosynthesis**, and soon afterwards oxygen began to appear in the atmosphere. **Over the next billion years plants evolved** and the percentage of oxygen **gradually increased**, eventually reaching a level that **enabled animals to evolve**.

Photosynthesis is worth highlighting because it explains **two** changes at once. The equation

$$\mathrm{6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2}$$

shows carbon dioxide being **taken in** and oxygen being **given out**, so the fall of one and the rise of the other are two halves of the same process rather than two separate stories.

Carbon dioxide was removed in a third way as well: by the **formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels that contain carbon**. **Limestone** formed from the **shells and skeletons** of sea creatures; **coal** from **plant material** buried where it could not fully decay; **crude oil and natural gas** from **plankton** buried in mud under high pressure and temperature. The carbon was not destroyed but **locked away**.

**Nitrogen**, meanwhile, simply **accumulated**. It is very **unreactive**, so unlike carbon dioxide it had almost nothing to remove it. That is why it is now the most abundant gas — not because most was released, but because least was taken away.

The result is the atmosphere of the last **200 million years**: about **four-fifths (80%) nitrogen**, **one-fifth (20%) oxygen**, and **small proportions of other gases** including carbon dioxide, water vapour and the noble gases.

questions.prompt: Explain why scientists cannot be certain about the composition of the Earth's early atmosphere, and evaluate how useful the comparison with Mars and Venus is as evidence.
questions.skill: evaluating evidence about the early atmosphere
questions.solution:
Scientists cannot be certain about the early atmosphere because of the **timescale**. The Earth is about **4.6 billion years** old, and the period in question is its **first billion years**. There were no observers and no measurements, so there are **no direct records** of any kind. What physical evidence survives — rocks, trapped gases, mineral deposits — has been **altered** repeatedly by heat, pressure and chemical change over that enormous span. Every line of evidence is therefore **indirect**, and has to be interpreted rather than simply read.

This is why the specification is careful to say that **theories about what was in the Earth's early atmosphere and how it was formed have changed and developed over time**, and why answers should be phrased as *one theory suggests* rather than as settled fact.

The **comparison with Mars and Venus** is one of the more useful pieces of indirect evidence. Both planets today have atmospheres that are **mainly carbon dioxide** with **little or no oxygen** — precisely what the theory proposes for the early Earth. All three planets formed at **similar times** and in **similar ways**, from the same region of the solar system, so it is reasonable to expect their early atmospheres to have been alike. Mars and Venus also lack the two things that transformed Earth's atmosphere — **liquid oceans** and **life** — which makes them, in effect, a picture of what Earth might have stayed like. That the comparison points the same way as other evidence, such as the composition of volcanic gases, strengthens it further, since evidence from **more than one independent source** is harder to dismiss.

But the comparison **supports without confirming**. The three planets differ in ways that matter: **size**, and therefore gravity and the ability to retain gases; **temperature** and **distance from the Sun**, which determine whether water is liquid, frozen or vapour; and geological history. Venus is far hotter than Earth ever was, and Mars is far colder and much smaller. Any of those differences could have produced a different early atmosphere, so the similarity may be partly coincidental.

On balance, the comparison is **worth having but not decisive**. It makes the theory more **plausible**, and it agrees with other indirect evidence, which is what good evidence should do. It cannot **prove** the composition of Earth's early atmosphere, because no evidence available to us can — and that limitation, rather than any weakness in the reasoning, is the real answer to the question.

examTechnique.body:
Half of this topic is recall of a **story with figures** — 80% and 20%, 4.6 billion years, 2.7 billion years, 200 million years — and half is a **skills** question about evidence.

For the story, keep hold of the causes rather than the sequence: **volcanoes** put the gases there, the **oceans** and **photosynthesis** and **burial** took the carbon dioxide out, **photosynthesis** put the oxygen in, and **nitrogen accumulated because nothing removed it**.
examinerErrors: Giving only **photosynthesis** when asked how carbon dioxide decreased, and omitting the **oceans** and **burial in rocks and fuels**.
Saying nitrogen is abundant because **volcanoes released the most**, rather than because it is **unreactive**.
Stating the early atmosphere as **fact** rather than as what **one theory suggests**.
Forgetting the comparison with **Mars and Venus**, which the specification names.
Confusing the origins of **coal** (plants), **crude oil and gas** (plankton) and **limestone** (shells and skeletons).
Listing points in an **evaluate** question without reaching a **judgement**.
Giving the proportions the wrong way round: nitrogen is **four-fifths**, oxygen **one-fifth**.
Saying the carbon **disappeared**, rather than being **locked into** rocks and fossil fuels.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer uses **photosynthesis** to explain the fall of carbon dioxide and the rise of oxygen **together**, because it is one equation. It explains nitrogen's abundance by what **did not** happen to it. It says where the carbon **went** — limestone, coal, oil and gas — and then draws the consequence: burning fossil fuels **returns** carbon that took millions of years to remove. On evidence it writes *one theory suggests*, names the **4.6 billion year** timescale as the reason, and when asked to evaluate the Mars and Venus comparison it gives what it **supports**, what it **cannot settle**, and a **judgement** with the reason attached.
